title: Lot 1, Your Chats
concept: Character.AI, an app where people talk with AI characters, filed for bankruptcy in October and plans to auction its assets on December 1st. Per the attorneys general it collects private chats, voice calls and mental health disclosures and uses them to train its AI, and the data could pass to a new owner. A $10 million starting bid covers the app, its AI models, user accounts and chat content; Disney's $20 million is for a technology license, not the chats. Alaska joined a bipartisan coalition of 40 attorneys general led by New York, and per Alaska's Department of Law the court ordered a consumer privacy ombudsman at the coalition's urging. The U.S. Trustee named Lucy Thomson. She reviews the planned sale and recommends safeguards, weighing the policy, what users could lose or gain and alternatives. The $10 million bidder was formed the day before the filing that disclosed its bid and its backer isn't public. The company says its policy already allowed the sale; Alaska argues the limits on minors are voluntary and a buyer could reverse them. The ombudsman advises and the court decides. Drawn as Scrollback, a faced accordion of chat bubbles whose scarf of older messages squares off into crates on an auction platform, a lot tag that changes face, two bidder stands (DISNEY and a blank card), and an empty brass scale the ombudsman fills herself before handing her binder up to the court.

treatment.title: Lot 1, Your Chats
treatment.summary: Lot 1, Your Chats (Explainer winner with grafts, restaged at Gate 0B). SCROLLBACK, a chat history drawn as an accordion of rounded chat bubbles with a worried face on its pale mint top bubble, pops out of a phone on an Anchorage kitchen table at night (snowy Chugach in the window, a moose squinting in) and a mustard lot tag THUNKs onto its foot. Inside the phone a flat chat window shows user and AI bubbles, one wearing a THERAPIST? badge; the bubbles extrude into Scrollback's scarf, which unspools and squares off into labelled crates, one sliding into a MODEL hopper. A dashed map line carries the tagged crates from Alaska to a tiny Delaware courtroom; on the auction floor a $10M starburst lands on the tag, a spotlight finds two bidder stands (DISNEY and a blank name card), and Disney's grey crate steps up to its own stand with only a tech license. Alaska's flag snaps up at the front of a row of attorneys general desks, New York's lamp lights and 39 follow, and the light runs out the doors to the court, where a gavel orders an ombudsman and a clerk sets an empty brass scale down. A faceless Lucy Thomson pins on her badge, opens her binder and seals the lot tag SAFEGUARDS?. The camera slides to the blank name card as the tag flips to FORMED NOV 13 · BID FILED NOV 14. The company's case gets full strength (a lawyer unrolls the policy with both hands, TOLD THE COURT, a highlighted clause, a checked box, PER THE COMPANY), then Alaska's argument (a sticky note on a crate that a dashed outline shows could tear off). She sets each weight into the scale herself, the beam never settling, slides her blank-covered binder into the court's tray and steps back as a gavel twice the scale's size descends. Hard cut on the tag to the kitchen: COURT DECIDES over an empty signature line, a calendar with DEC 1 circled, and a rise to the Chugach.
treatment.judge_reasoning: Reasoning: SCROLLBACK's design IS conversation history (scarf of older messages unspools into labeled crates); avoids paper-slip and metal-fixture idioms; cake turn shows "formed two days before" with no smear; tag ends on the court's empty signature line.

angle.thesis: When an AI company fails, the chats people gave it become something to sell, and the coalition Alaska joined got a privacy expert in front of the court before that sale, which matters most because the money behind the bid for the chats has no public name and the court, not the expert, decides.
angle.falsifiability: False if the chats are pulled from the sale before the hearing (then they were never really for sale, c10), or if the court approves the transfer without weighing any safeguard the ombudsman recommends (then the expert in the room changed nothing, c16, c17, c26), or if the bidder's backer turns out to be public and accountable already (c11).
supporting_facts: Chats are an asset. Per the attorneys general the company collects private chats, voice calls and mental health disclosures and uses them to train its AI (c6, c7), the data could pass to a new owner through bankruptcy (c8), and the $10M starting bid covers the app, the AI models, user accounts and chat content (c10), with an auction planned December 1st (c9).

Alaska got a real procedural result. Alaska joined the coalition in October (c13), New York led with 39 others (c14), and at the coalition's urging the court ordered a consumer privacy ombudsman (c15), now Lucy Thomson, named by the U.S. Trustee (c19), who reviews the sale and recommends safeguards (c16) weighing the policy, what users could lose or gain, and alternatives that cut the losses (c18).

The open variable is the buyer. The starting bidder for the chats was formed the day before the filing that disclosed its bid and its backer isn't public (c11), while Disney's $20M bid is for a technology license, not the chats (c12).
angle.counterpoint_to_honor: The company's fair case gets a full scene. Character.AI told the court its privacy policy already allowed the sale (c25, attributed, single source), the statute itself asks what users could GAIN as well as lose (c18), and the ombudsman can't block anything, she advises and the court decides (c17), after a hearing (c26). The state's own worry, that the limits on minors are voluntary and a buyer could reverse them (c22), is the state's argument, not a finding, and the appointment doesn't settle it.
angle.who_it_serves: Alaskans who use AI chat apps, families (c5, self-declared under 18 accounts per the NY AG), Alaska's Department of Law judged on what joining a coalition actually bought, and Alaska builders who need users to trust what happens to their data.
angle.second_movement: Act 2 turns the privacy win into a question: the expert is in the room, but the bidder for the chats is a shell formed two days before its bid and its backer has no name (c11). Act 3 is the test, the company's case drawn at full strength: users clicked yes to a policy the company says already allowed this (c25), and the law itself counts gains (c18). The film survives by narrowing: the expert doesn't stop the sale, she makes the terms visible to the one who decides.
angle.button: The ombudsman advises. The court decides. And the money behind the bid for the chats, so far, has no name.

runner_up_angles.thesis: Your chats are a transferable asset, so AI confidence needs privacy rules that bind the next owner (analyst A).
runner_up_angles.why_lost: a policy prescription no claim states and it put the ombudsman in charge; its 'chats become inventory' mechanism is the winner's first act

runner_up_angles.thesis: Alaska got a real result that is procedural, not final (analyst B).
runner_up_angles.why_lost: implied Alaska led and assumed a counterfactual; its credit to the coalition and its naming of the expert are folded in

runner_up_angles.thesis: The ombudsman is the price of entry, the question is who buys and on what terms (analyst C).
runner_up_angles.why_lost: too close to the company's framing and dropped the coalition; its unnamed-buyer turn is the winner's second movement and button
